en: If hosts came flooding against him,
He never panicked or hurried.
If a formidable foe fell into his hands,
He crushed him into a patch the size of a rabbit.
Though ninety armies grappled with him,
He never opened his flank in fear.
They drew their mighty bows,
And shot at one another with thudding blows,
Standing amid battle cries,
Fighting without sparing their lives.
All their spears shattered.
Every coat of mail was torn apart,
And each lion’s valor was revealed;
All their robes were ripped,
All their gear burst asunder.
They seized each other by the collar,
And sank waist-deep into the earth.
They took no rest by day,
Nor any rest by night.
They fought through days and nights—
Who had ever seen such a deed?
Both armies stood motionless,
Unable to advance, as though paralyzed.
Their poor heads, once full of life,
Became buckets of crimson blood.
Axe-bearing Sarybai
Came upon him in fury.
He swung his cast-iron mace, huge as a house,
Pouring all his rage into it,
Gripped it in both hands and let it fly,
Turning his warhorse’s head,
And struck with all his might.
The shield burned and became an ember;
What could poor Choro do?
His eyes blazed like fire.
The gray racer’s back was broken,
All its bones cracking,
Its fly-like soul shrieking.
Choro collapsed unconscious,
His two eyes rolling,
His fine mustache twisted,
His flashing eyes staring wide.
Stricken by grievous pain,
His insides seethed like embers,
His two eyes became fire,
And his whole body trembled.
When he faced forward and leveled his spear,
His back had failed and he stooped,
His eyes bulging and staring.
His eyes flashed like a lion’s,
And against the infidel son of a monster,
Before a word could be spoken,
In the blink of an eye,
He arrived faster than an arrow.
As he reached the infidel,
Thinking, “Here is the face of the ribs,
Here is the very center of the lungs,
Here is where this raging swine
Will fall,”
Külchoro thrust his spear.
Such is the way of heroes:
They stood facing one another.
Thinking, “Here is the core of the fleshly heart,
The place between lung and heart,
The measured eye of death,
The very place where he must die,
Where he will wheel like a blue vulture
And his soul take flight,”
Sarybai thrust his spear.
The four-legged chargers
Collapsed side by side.
The spears that struck together
Shattered into fragments.
Such is the way of warriors:
They stood face-to-face.
Firing guns and drawing bows,
They fought with crashing blows.
They struck with battle-axes,
Until the axes shattered
And only the hafts remained in their hands.
They fought with swords,
Until every sword shattered
And only the hilts remained in their hands.
They stood on opposing slopes,
Fighting with battle-axes—
Who had ever seen such a deed?
He drank and gulped down blood.
Crushing the mighty,
My child, I fear he will slaughter us to the last.
Leaving not a hair of the Kyrgyz,
I fear he will pass through in massacre.
My child, will he knead us like dough,
Will he tear out our roots?
He will diminish our hopes,
Will he destroy the mighty?
He will wipe out the noble,
And unleash calamity and ruin.
Will this poor people gathered here,
Stripped of mane and tail,
Be left hornless?
With the horn broken from our brow,
Will we be left barren?
If this infidel continues so,
He will unleash terrible wrath;
Bride and widowed wife alike
Will abandon the village’s shelter…
Unable to match him in combat,
Fighting on without strength enough,
He will make girls and women widows,
And turn the mighty into slaves;
I fear he will destroy us all.
Sweeping away every last trace,
I fear he will leave us slaughtered.
The people wailed in anguish,
Despairing of their fly-like lives.
All the warriors groaned,
And the people despaired of life.
What will become of us in the end?
Not one of us will remain.
Our blood will flow like water,
And all of us will be massacred.
I fear he will utterly destroy us,
And now bind and carry off
The people who once lived in peace.
I fear he will crush and kill the leaders.
The one God, the Lord Most High,
Had grown wrathful, and Sarybai
Strode about roaring.
Every human creature’s
Whole body shuddered;
In furious anguish,
Every living creature
Despaired of its wretched life.
Your infidel son of a monster
Showed himself a demon;
His cavernous mouth opened,
And fiery, venomous breath
Sprayed from his mouth.
Everyone who saw him
Was broken in body and crushed.
The people wailed in anguish,
And the watching multitude said,
“Sarybai is a demon,”
Despairing of their fly-like lives.
Külchoro was a lion upheld by the saints,
A lion and tiger
Who had subdued the whole world.
For these Kyrgyz, Külchoro
Was an iron gate and fortress.
“God, preserve Choro!” they cried.
Hero Semetey wept blood,
The white-bearded elders wept,
All the common people wept;
All the nation grieved,
And the people despaired of life.
Would he slaughter the heroes and khans,
And destroy so many souls?
Would he exterminate them all together,
Leaving not a hair of living souls,
And depart after massacring them?
Sarybai was no man, but venom;
He was the great God’s wrath.
He bore a vengeance passed down from old,
The vengeance of Mader.
He mangled all who crossed him,
And devoured all whom he encountered.
“What dire hardship, what grievous plight!
What will become of the people?”
“The madman grows more violent,
And will suck out every soul.”
Külchoro was a lion upheld by the saints,
A hero fit to face the foe,
The very backbone of these Kyrgyz.
He was a khan like a leopard,
With the courage of a lion.
“Trample the many foes beneath your feet;
God, if you created him as a living soul,
Keep Külchoro safe!
If anything happens to Külchoro,
Our backbone will be broken,
And our people massacred.
Our lifeblood will burst forth—
Thus will our breath leave us.
We stand here with purpose;
Make this merely an age of trial fallen upon us.
God, if you created him as a living soul,
God, keep Choro safe!”
The nation clamored and cried out,
And the people despaired of life.
Your infidel son of a monster
Could not be reached by fired bullets;
Thrust spears could not pierce him,
Nor would engulfing flames burn him.
The madman was invulnerable;
None knew where his mortal spot lay.
His champions were unlike other men,
And brought calamity upon our poor heads.
He raged bewilderingly through battle,
Breaking seventy spears,
Exposing muscle to bullets.
Armor impervious to bullets was torn,
And from the bullet-defying gray colt
The valiant Külchoro was parted.
For seven days he ranged about,
Wounding all he reached,
Until strength and power were exhausted;
I fear he has found his chance and struck.
Spreading wrath among the multitude,
You have given us an enemy, one God!
A calamity and affliction to the nation—
You have given us an enemy, one God!
The Ala-Too where you made your home
Was never conquered by a foe.
While bloodthirsty Manas lived,
We were a people dwelling in peace.
On the plain of Jylgynduu,
Along the broad Talas,
We would divide a whole sable skin
Into two halves
And wrap them around our leggings.
When bored, we hunted roe deer;
Kumis by day and girls by night,
We reveled with thunderous joy.
Eating the fat colts of barren mares,
With vodka and feasts in winter,
We used to revel with loud cries.
When desire stirred, we stayed up all night,
Slaughtering mares and playing ordo,
Hunting in rain and flying our birds.
In whatever way we pleased—
Where are the nights that were like the Night of Power?
Where are the flowers that stood in bloom?
Where are those former days of flowering?
Sarybai was no man, but venom;
He was the true God’s wrath!
Against the sons of these Kyrgyz
He came as a living calamity.
What enmity could your scorched dog
Possibly bear us?
Lamenting, souls wept;
All the people bowed their heads and wept,
Even children too young to understand wept.
Sarybai upon the battlefield
Revealed the calamity within him;
Before this foreign infidel,
The people despaired of life.
The peoples of the world had been destroyed.
My renowned father was a lion,
Favored by perfect fortune.
As for the offspring born from him,
Unable to overcome Sarybai,
What sort of descendants could they be called?
Our first ancestor was Tügöl Khan;
You made all his line lions.
Yet unable to overcome this accursed one,
Allah Most High, one God,
